package com.thealgorithms.backtracking; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.List; /** * The Combination Sum problem is a classic backtracking algorithm problem * where we need to find all unique combinations of candidates that sum to * a given target value. * *

Problem Statement:
* Given an array of distinct integers (candidates) and a target integer, * find all unique combinations where the candidate numbers sum to the target. * The same number may be used unlimited number of times.

* *

Key Characteristics:

*
    *
  • Candidates are distinct positive integers
    • *
  • Same number can be used multiple times (unlimited reuse)
    • *
  • All combinations must be unique (no duplicate combinations)
    • *
  • Order of numbers in each combination does not matter
    • *
  • All numbers in candidates are positive
    • *
* *

Algorithm Approach:
* Uses backtracking with a pick/not-pick strategy and allows reuse of candidates. * Sorting helps with pruning and ensuring uniqueness of combinations.

* *

Example Usage:

* 
 * // Find combinations that sum to 7 using candidates [2, 3, 6, 7]
 * int[] candidates = {2, 3, 6, 7};
 * List<List<Integer>> combinations = CombinationSum.findCombinations(candidates, 7);
 * // Result: [[2, 2, 3], [7]]
 * 
 * // Find combinations that sum to 8 using candidates [2, 3, 5]
 * int[] nums = {2, 3, 5};
 * List<List<Integer>> results = CombinationSum.findCombinations(nums, 8);
 * // Result: [[2, 2, 2, 2], [2, 3, 3], [3, 5]]
 *
* *

Time Complexity: O(N^(T/M + 1)) where N is the number of candidates, * T is the target, and M is the minimal value among candidates. * In worst case, this can be exponential.

* *

Space Complexity: O(T/M) for the recursion stack, * plus O(number_of_combinations × average_combination_length) for storing results.

* * @see Backtracking (Wikipedia) * @see LeetCode Problem 39 - Combination Sum */ public final class CombinationSum { // Private constructor to prevent instantiation (utility class) private CombinationSum() { throw new UnsupportedOperationException("This is a utility class and cannot be instantiated"); } /** * Finds all unique combinations that sum to the target value. * *

The algorithm works by: *

    *
  1. Sorting candidates to enable pruning and ensure consistent ordering
    2. *
  2. Using backtracking to explore inclusion/exclusion of each candidate
    3. *
  3. Allowing unlimited reuse of the same candidate
    4. *
  4. Pruning branches where candidates exceed remaining target
    5. *
*

* * @param candidateNumbers Array of distinct positive integers to choose from * @param targetSum The target sum to achieve with the combinations * @return A list containing all unique combinations that sum to the target * @throws IllegalArgumentException if candidateNumbers contains non-positive numbers * * @example * findCombinations(new int[]{2,3,5}, 8) → [[2,2,2,2], [2,3,3], [3,5]] * findCombinations(new int[]{2}, 1) → [] * findCombinations(new int[]{1,2}, 3) → [[1,1,1], [1,2]] */ public static List> findCombinations(int[] candidateNumbers, int targetSum) { // Validate input if (candidateNumbers == null) { throw new IllegalArgumentException("Candidate numbers array cannot be null"); } List> allCombinations = new ArrayList<>(); // Early return for empty array if (candidateNumbers.length == 0) { return allCombinations; } // Validate all numbers are positive for (int number : candidateNumbers) { if (number <= 0) { throw new IllegalArgumentException( "All candidate numbers must be positive integers. Found: " + number ); } } // Sort candidates to enable pruning and ensure combinations are generated in order int[] sortedCandidates = candidateNumbers.clone(); Arrays.sort(sortedCandidates); // Start the backtracking process findCombinationsRecursive(sortedCandidates, targetSum, 0, new ArrayList<>(), allCombinations); return allCombinations; } /** * Recursive backtracking method that builds combinations. * *

This method implements the core logic: *

    *
  • If remaining target becomes 0, we found a valid combination
    • *
  • Try including each candidate from the current position onward
    • *
  • Since the array is sorted, if candidate > remaining, we can break
    • *
  • Allow reuse of the same candidate by not incrementing the index
    • *
*

* * @param sortedCandidates Pre-sorted array of candidate numbers * @param remainingTarget The remaining sum to achieve * @param startIndex The index from which to start selecting candidates (ensures combinations are generated in order) * @param currentCombination The current combination being built * @param allCombinations List to store all valid combinations found */ private static void findCombinationsRecursive(int[] sortedCandidates, int remainingTarget, int startIndex, List currentCombination, List> allCombinations) { // Base case: We've achieved the exact target sum if (remainingTarget == 0) { // Found a valid combination - store a copy allCombinations.add(new ArrayList<>(currentCombination)); return; } // Try all candidates from startIndex onward for (int candidateIndex = startIndex; candidateIndex < sortedCandidates.length; candidateIndex++) { int currentCandidate = sortedCandidates[candidateIndex]; // Pruning: Since array is sorted, if current candidate exceeds remaining target, // all subsequent candidates will also exceed (they're larger) if (currentCandidate > remainingTarget) { break; // No need to check further candidates } // CHOOSE: Include the current candidate in our combination currentCombination.add(currentCandidate); // EXPLORE: Recurse to find more numbers to complete the sum // Pass the same index (not i+1) because we can reuse the same element findCombinationsRecursive(sortedCandidates, remainingTarget - currentCandidate, candidateIndex, // Note: index stays the same (reuse allowed) currentCombination, allCombinations); // UNCHOOSE: Backtrack by removing the last element currentCombination.remove(currentCombination.size() - 1); } } /** * Variation of combination sum where each candidate can only be used once. * This is the "Combination Sum II" problem. * * @param candidateNumbers Array of candidates (may contain duplicates) * @param targetSum The target sum to achieve * @return A list containing all unique combinations (each candidate used at most once) */ public static List> findCombinationsWithoutReuse(int[] candidateNumbers, int targetSum) { if (candidateNumbers == null || candidateNumbers.length == 0) { return new ArrayList<>(); } // Sort to handle duplicates and enable pruning int[] sortedCandidates = candidateNumbers.clone(); Arrays.sort(sortedCandidates); List> allCombinations = new ArrayList<>(); findCombinationsWithoutReuseRecursive(sortedCandidates, targetSum, 0, new ArrayList<>(), allCombinations); return allCombinations; } /** * Recursive method for combinations without reuse. * Similar to findCombinationsRecursive but increments index to prevent reuse. * * @param sortedCandidates Pre-sorted array of candidates * @param remainingTarget Remaining target sum * @param startIndex Current position to start from * @param currentCombination Current combination being built * @param allCombinations List to store results */ private static void findCombinationsWithoutReuseRecursive(int[] sortedCandidates, int remainingTarget, int startIndex, List currentCombination, List> allCombinations) { if (remainingTarget == 0) { allCombinations.add(new ArrayList<>(currentCombination)); return; } for (int candidateIndex = startIndex; candidateIndex < sortedCandidates.length; candidateIndex++) { int currentCandidate = sortedCandidates[candidateIndex]; // Skip duplicates to avoid duplicate combinations if (candidateIndex > startIndex && sortedCandidates[candidateIndex] == sortedCandidates[candidateIndex - 1]) { continue; } if (currentCandidate > remainingTarget) { break; // Prune since array is sorted } currentCombination.add(currentCandidate); // Pass i+1 because we can't reuse the same element findCombinationsWithoutReuseRecursive(sortedCandidates, remainingTarget - currentCandidate, candidateIndex + 1, currentCombination, allCombinations); currentCombination.remove(currentCombination.size() - 1); } } /** * Returns the number of combinations without generating them. * This is useful for estimating result size before computation. * * @param candidates Array of candidate numbers * @param target The target sum * @return The number of possible combinations (estimation, not exact for large inputs) */ public static int estimateCombinationCount(int[] candidates, int target) { if (candidates == null || candidates.length == 0) { return 0; } // This is a rough estimation - exact count calculation is also exponential // For exact count, we would need to perform the backtracking anyway return (int) Math.pow(target / candidates[0], candidates.length); } /** * Utility method to print all combinations in a readable format. * * @param combinations The list of combinations to print */ public static void printAllCombinations(List> combinations) { if (combinations == null || combinations.isEmpty()) { System.out.println("No combinations found."); return; } System.out.println("Found " + combinations.size() + " combination(s):"); for (int combinationIndex = 0; combinationIndex < combinations.size(); combinationIndex++) { System.out.printf("Combination %d: %s%n", combinationIndex + 1, combinations.get(combinationIndex)); } } } /* COMPREHENSIVE DOCUMENTATION =========================== ALGORITHM DEEP DIVE ------------------- Problem Understanding: ====================== Given: candidates = [2, 3, 6, 7], target = 7 Valid Combinations: - 2 + 2 + 3 = 7 → [2, 2, 3] - 7 = 7 → [7] - Other attempts: 2+2+2+2=8 (exceeds), 3+3=6 (not enough) Why Sorting Helps? ================= 1. Pruning: Once candidate > remaining, break the loop 2. Ordering: Ensures combinations are generated in lexicographic order 3. Duplicate prevention: Makes it easy to skip duplicates Backtracking Tree Visualization (target=7, candidates=[2,3,6,7]) ============================================================== root(7) | +-----------------+-----------------+ | | | | 2(5) 3(4) 6(1) 7(0)✓ | | | +----+----+----+ +----+----+ +------+ | | | | | | | | | 2(3) 3(2) 6(-1)7(-2) 2(2) 3(1) 6(-2) 2(-1) 3(-2) ... (pruned) | | | ... 2(0)✓ ... | [2,2,3]✓ LEGEND: - (n) = remaining target after adding candidate - ✓ = valid combination found - Pruned branches not shown RECURSION DEPTH ANALYSIS ======================== | Target | Min Candidate | Max Depth | Example | |--------|--------------|-----------|---------| | 100 | 1 | 100 | Using all 1's | | 100 | 5 | 20 | Using all 5's | | 50 | 2 | 25 | Using all 2's | | Target | min(candidates) | target/min(candidates) | OPTIMIZATION TECHNIQUES ======================= 1. Sorting + Pruning: - Reduces branches by eliminating impossible paths early - Break loop when candidate > remaining 2. Start Index Parameter: - Prevents generating duplicate permutations - Ensures combinations are built in non-decreasing order 3. Early Termination: - Return immediately when remaining == 0 - Skip candidates that would exceed target 4. Array Cloning: - Preserves original input array - Allows safe sorting without modifying input PERFORMANCE COMPARISON ====================== | Approach | Time Complexity | Space Complexity | When to Use | |----------|----------------|------------------|-------------| | Recursive Backtracking | O(N^(T/M)) | O(T/M) | Standard solution | | DP with memoization | O(N × T) | O(N × T) | For single use, larger T | | BFS approach | O(N^(T/M)) | O(N^(T/M)) | When all combinations needed | | Iterative with stack | O(N^(T/M)) | O(T/M) | To avoid recursion depth | COMMON VARIANTS =============== 1. Combination Sum I (this implementation): - Unlimited reuse of candidates - All numbers are distinct - Return all combinations 2. Combination Sum II: - Each candidate can be used only once - Input may contain duplicates - Need to skip duplicates in same level 3. Combination Sum III: - Find combinations of size k - Numbers from 1 to 9 only - No reuse allowed 4. Combination Sum IV: - Count number of combinations (different order counts) - Usually solved with DP - Different from permutations count PRACTICAL APPLICATIONS ====================== 1. Coin Change Problem - Find ways to make change for a given amount - Unlimited coins with denominations 2. Number Partitioning - Split numbers into subsets with equal sum - Resource allocation optimization 3. Budget Allocation - Find combinations of items within budget - Shopping cart optimization 4. Investment Portfolio - Combine investments to reach target return - Risk management constraints 5. Chemical Formulation - Combine chemicals in specific ratios - Achieve target mixture composition 6. Game Development - Find combinations of moves to achieve score - Puzzle-solving mechanics 7. Manufacturing - Combine parts to meet production quota - Inventory management COMPLEXITY ANALYSIS DETAILS ========================== Time Complexity Breakdown: ------------------------- Let: - N = number of candidates - T = target value - M = minimum candidate value The recursion tree has: - Maximum depth: T/M - Branching factor: up to N - Total nodes: roughly N^(T/M) - Work per node: O(1) Therefore: O(N^(T/M)) Space Complexity Breakdown: ------------------------ 1. Recursion stack: O(T/M) 2. Current combination storage: O(T/M) 3. Result storage: O(C × L) where: - C = number of valid combinations - L = average length of each combination EDGE CASES ========== | Case | Input | Expected Output | |------|-------|-----------------| | Target < smallest candidate | [2,3], target=1 | [] | | Target equals candidate | [2,3], target=2 | [[2]] | | Target = 0 | [1,2], target=0 | [] or [[]] depending on spec | | Single candidate | [5], target=10 | [[5,5]] | | All candidates > target | [6,7,8], target=5 | [] | DEBUGGING TIPS ============== 1. Print remaining target at each recursion level 2. Trace the combination being built 3. Verify pruning conditions work correctly 4. Check that start index parameter is correctly maintained 5. Ensure copies of combinations are made when adding to results FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS ========================== Q: Why do we sort the array? A: Sorting enables the pruning optimization and ensures combinations are generated in non-decreasing order, which prevents duplicates. Q: Why do we use start index instead of visited set? A: Using start index ensures we only consider elements from current position onward, which automatically prevents duplicate combinations. Q: Why do we pass i (not i+1) in the recursive call? A: Passing i (same index) allows reuse of the same element multiple times. For problems without reuse, we pass i+1. Q: How to handle negative numbers? A: This algorithm assumes all numbers are positive. Negative numbers complicate the problem because the sum could go up and down. For negative numbers, you cannot use the same pruning optimization. Q: Can this be solved iteratively? A: Yes, using a stack to simulate recursion, but recursive solution is more intuitive for backtracking problems. RELATED ALGORITHMS ================= 1. package com.thealgorithms.bitmanipulation;

/**
 * A utility class to swap every pair of adjacent bits in a given integer.
 * This operation shifts the even-positioned bits to odd positions and vice versa.
 *
 * Example:
 * - Input: 2 (binary: `10`) → Output: 1 (binary: `01`)
 * - Input: 43 (binary: `101011`) → Output: 23 (binary: `010111`)
 *
 * **Explanation of the Algorithm:**
 * 1. Mask even-positioned bits: Using `0xAAAAAAAA` (binary: `101010...`),
 *    which selects bits in even positions.
 * 2. Mask odd-positioned bits: Using `0x55555555` (binary: `010101...`),
 *    which selects bits in odd positions.
 * 3. Shift bits:
 *    - Right-shift even-positioned bits by 1 to move them to odd positions.
 *    - Left-shift odd-positioned bits by 1 to move them to even positions.
 * 4. Combine both shifted results using bitwise OR (`|`) to produce the final result.
 *
 * Use Case: This algorithm can be useful in applications involving low-level bit manipulation,
 * such as encoding, data compression, or cryptographic transformations.
 *
 * Time Complexity: O(1) (constant time, since operations are bitwise).
 *
 * Author: Lakshyajeet Singh Goyal (https://github.com/DarkMatter-999)
 */
public final class SwapAdjacentBits {
private SwapAdjacentBits() {
}

/**
 * Swaps every pair of adjacent bits of a given integer.
 * Steps:
 * 1. Mask the even-positioned bits.
 * 2. Mask the odd-positioned bits.
 * 3. Shift the even bits to the right and the odd bits to the left.
 * 4. Combine the shifted bits.
 *
 * @param originalNumber the integer whose bits are to be swapped
 * @return the integer after swapping every pair of adjacent bits
 */
public static int swapAdjacentBits(int originalNumber) {
int evenPositionBits = originalNumber & 0xAAAAAAAA;
int oddPositionBits = originalNumber & 0x55555555;
evenPositionBits >>= 1;
oddPositionBits <<= 1;
return evenPositionBits | oddPositionBits;
}
}

package com.thealgorithms.datastructures.lists; /** * The SearchSinglyLinkedListRecursion class extends SinglyLinkedList and provides * a method to search for a value in a singly linked list using recursion. *

* This class demonstrates a recursive approach to check if a given integer value is * present in the linked list. The search method calls a private recursive helper method * `searchRecursion`, which checks each node's value and moves to the next node if necessary. *

*

* Example: * Given a list containing the values 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4, calling search(3) will return `true`, * while calling search(5) will return `false`. *

*

* Complexity: *

    *
  • Time Complexity: O(n), where n is the number of nodes in the linked list.
    • *
  • Space Complexity: O(n), due to the recursive call stack in the worst case.
    • *
*

*/ public class SearchSinglyLinkedListRecursion extends SinglyLinkedList { /** * Recursively searches for a given value in the linked list. * * @param node the head node to start the search. * @param key the integer value to be searched for. * @return {@code true} if the value `key` is present in the list; otherwise, {@code false}. */ private boolean searchRecursion(SinglyLinkedListNode node, int key) { return (node != null && (node.value == key || searchRecursion(node.next, key))); } /** * Public search method to determine if a key is present in the linked list. * * @param key the integer value to be searched for. * @return {@code true} if the value `key` is present in the list; otherwise, {@code false}. */ @Override public boolean search(int key) { return searchRecursion(getHead(), key); } }
